newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian focus turns to IMF after election.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian focus turns to IMF after election.

text.p: Opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov won a decisive victory over the ruling ex-communists in Bulgaria's weekend presidential election, latest figures showed on Monday.
But financial markets were already paying more attention to a visiting IMF mission which may well determine the country's ability to stay solvent.
The International Monetary Fund mission must decide whether to grant Bulgaria $115 million in fresh credit. If it refuses, the country could default on its $10 billion foreign debt.
The Bulgarian lev fell to 246-247 per dollar on the interbank market on Monday morning from at 244-245 at Friday's close on rumours the funds might be denied, dealers said.
Markets discounted Sunday's presidential run-off but newspapers hailed the result and urged Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov to resign.

With most votes counted, official preliminary results gave Stoyanov, a pro-reform lawyer of the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) 59.9 percent of the vote to Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov's 40.1 percent.

Although the president is a largely ceremonial figure with limited powers, the scale of Stoyanov's victory threw the government onto the defensive and Videnov, battling a deep economic crisis, promised to take note.
IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk met Videnov on Sunday night. Officials described the talks as preliminary.
On her arrival on Friday, McGuirk said the IMF was concerned that Bulgaria's corruption prevented a normal market economy from developing.
Videnov, in power for nearly two years, said on Sunday a party congress could be held as early as January to review policy and did not rule out cabinet changes.
"Petar Stoyanov's crushing victory is the biggest blow for Zhan Videnov since he became prime minister. He has to resign," said the daily Standart in a front-page editorial.
The electoral commission put turnout at 61 percent, close to last week's first round 63 percent.

Videnov, often criticised for his secretive and authoritarian style of government, has presided over a big drop in living standards as Bulgaria struggles to meet foreign debt payments and carry out long-delayed reforms.
"Bulgarians have declared their desire for change, even though the institution of president lacks any real power to alter the country's course," said Novinar newspaper.

Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, who did not stand for re-election, frequently wielded his veto over Socialist legislation, frustrating what he saw as government attempts to restore communist-era practices.
Stoyanov has pledged to bring Bulgaria -- which still looks to Moscow, its historical patron, for guidance -- closer to the European Union and NATO.

Stoyanov was careful on Sunday night to avoid direct criticism of the Socialists and proposed a National Salvation Council of experts and respected public figures to advise the government on how to avert economic collapse.

Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, which also held elections on Sunday, face similar difficulties but Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment among the former communist states of eastern Europe.
Bulgaria has managed to privatise only five percent of state industry since the bloodless overthrow of its communist regime seven years ago.
